dedupe_keys.name: machine learning urban temperatures and residential energy under heat mitigation los angeles

description: This study presents open-source, computationally efficient machine learning methods that improve urban temperature estimates relative to historical reanalysis data, and applies them to residential buildings in Los Angeles to compare the energy benefit of heat mitigation strategies with the effect of climate change. The authors frame urban heat as a driver of heat-related death and illness and of cooling demand, and note that estimating it is usually limited by coarse descriptions of the built environment, computational cost and a lack of high-resolution climate change estimates. Coverage: Los Angeles residential buildings. Access: arXiv preprint. Licence: arXiv preprint terms. Caveats: a preprint; the code repository is described as open source but was not linked on the abstract page. Outcome: cooling demand rises substantially by mid-century, engineered high-albedo surfaces could reduce the increase by more than 50 percent, and with electric heat pumps total annual heating and cooling energy still benefits from the cooling strategies. Simulation uses: pairing downscaled urban temperature with building energy models to appraise cool surfaces and electrification. Related records: the Houston heat mitigation study, ResStock and EnergyPlus.

name: Machine learning urban temperatures and residential energy under heat mitigation, Los Angeles
organisations: Grant Buster, Jordan Cox, Brandon N. Benton and Ryan N. King (authors)
outcomes: Cooling demand in Los Angeles homes is likely to rise substantially by mid-century, engineered high-albedo surfaces could cut that increase by more than half, and total heating plus cooling energy with electric heat pumps still benefits from the cooling measures despite higher heating demand.
